A research centre for rice founded in 1960 at Los Baños in the Philippines. Its rice variety IR8, released in 1966, launched the Green Revolution in Asia.

The Rockefeller and Ford foundations set it up with the Philippine government. Asia's population was growing fast and many feared famine. Breeders crossed a tall Indonesian rice with a short variety from Taiwan. The result, IR8, had short, stiff stems that could carry heavy heads of grain without falling over when fed with fertiliser.

With water and fertiliser, IR8 could yield several times as much as traditional rice. Farmers in the Philippines, India, Indonesia and beyond took it up, alongside the new wheats bred by Norman Borlaug in Mexico. Rice output rose faster than population, and the predicted famines did not come.

The gains had costs: more chemicals, more water and the loss of many old local varieties. IRRI now keeps one of the world's largest rice seed banks and breeds rice that survives floods, drought and salt. It follows a long line of rice advances going back to Champa rice.
